Missing Maryland man with Alzheimer’s shows up in Philadelphia, plays a piano
Musician with Alzheimer's found safely after driving from Maryland to Pennsylvania
78-year-old musician with Alzheimer’s found 100 miles from home playing piano after mysterious disappearance
sources.text:
A missing-person search involving a 78-year-old Maryland musician ended with an unexpected moment of music and kindness in Philadelphia. Frank Grow, who has been living with Alzheimer's disease for approximately six years, was found safe after travelling more than 100 miles from home. While his family was desperately looking for him, a stranger discovered him playing an abandoned piano in his front yard.
What made the incident particularly moving was that Grow, despite experiencing memory difficulties, could still play the instrument he had spent years performing on. His musical abilities helped turn a frightening situation into an emotional reunion.
How did Frank Grow disappear from his Maryland home?
According to the missing-person announcement issued by the Bowie Police Department on November 19, Grow had left his home in a Nissan Sentra. His daughter, Maggie Henkin, who cares for him, was briefly inside the house getting a cup of coffee when he drove away.
During her interviews with NBC Philadelphia and NBC Washington, Henkin recalled how quickly the situation unfolded.
"I was gone for literally two minutes, and when I came back out, the car was gone," Henkin said. "I just panicked. I didn’t know how far he had gotten."
Sitting beside her during the interviews, Grow offered his own explanation, saying, "I was headed away from where I was."
The family was left worried about his whereabouts until a resident in Philadelphia came across him several hours later.
An abandoned piano helped reconnect Frank Grow with music
Philadelphia resident Angelo Torres noticed Grow looking disoriented on his street. Concerned about the elderly man's condition, he approached him to find out whether he needed assistance.
"I pulled up to him, and I said, ‘Sir, are you okay? And he said, ‘No, I’m not okay," Torres told NBC Washington.
As Torres tried to help him, an abandoned piano sitting in his yard caught Grow's attention. The former musician sat down and began playing the instrument, displaying a familiar skill despite his difficulties navigating the unfamiliar surroundings.
Torres captured the unexpected moment on video. Introducing the elderly man, he said, "That’s my friend, Frank," before adding, "I just met him," as Grow smiled towards the camera.
Meeting him showed just how much music was still part of Grow's life, even after his Alzheimer's diagnosis.
How did Angelo Torres contact Grow's daughter?
Torres had found him, but he still had to figure out who he was and how to reach his family. He checked Grow for ID first, but came up empty. Then he searched the Nissan Sentra and finally turned up an old invoice in the trunk with Henkin's phone number on it.
The discovery made it possible to contact the family.
Recalling the unexpected call in her interview with NBC Philadelphia, Henkin said, "Around 1, I got a call from an unknown Philadelphia number, and I picked up and it was this man named Angelo, and he asked if I knew who Frank was. And I said, ‘Yes, that’s my dad,’"
She also remembered hearing her father speaking in the background when Torres called.
"When Angelo called, I heard my dad in the background saying, ‘Oh, I really did it this time,’" she added, per NBC Washington.
Once he was reunited with his family, Grow explained that he had been trying to reach his childhood home in Norristown, Pennsylvania. His journey had taken him much farther than he intended.
Why was the reunion emotional for both families?
Henkin was so relieved to find her dad safe after such a scary situation. Expressing her gratitude to the stranger who helped, she said, "I’m just so grateful and thankful. It was truly a miracle, and I’m so grateful for Angelo, and there are still good people out there."
The incident also carried a personal meaning for Torres. He revealed that he had lost his own father around the same time Grow was diagnosed with Alzheimer's. The unexpected meeting made him think about his father and the connection they had shared.
"All week I was thinking about my dad, and then all of a sudden he shows up, and I’m thinking my dad came in this form. That’s what I’m thinking," Torres said.
What began as a worrying disappearance ended with a family reunion, thanks to one person's decision to help. Grow's story also highlights the lasting place music can hold in someone's life and how a simple act of kindness can make an extraordinary difference.

sources.news_title: Alzheimer’s-Stricken Elderly Pianist Finds Piano on Philadelphia Street After Crossing Two States Searching for Childhood Home
sources.text:
An elderly Maryland pianist living with Alzheimer’s drove more than 100 miles while trying to find his childhood home in Pennsylvania. His unexpected journey ended on a Northeast Philadelphia street, where a Good Samaritan helped bring him safely back to his family.
Frank Grow, 78, disappeared from his home in Bowie on Thursday after setting out to locate the Norristown house where he grew up, according to NBC Philadelphia. Grow has been living with Alzheimer’s disease for six years.
Instead of reaching Norristown, Grow found himself in Northeast Philadelphia. That is where Angelo Torres noticed the confused musician near an intersection.
“I noticed a gentleman standing on the corner,” Torres told NBC10.
“So I pulled up to him and asked, ‘Sir, are you okay?’ And he replied, ‘No, I’m not okay.’”
Torres quickly understood that something was wrong. He searched Grow’s vehicle for identification or any information that could help locate his family.
“I started checking the car and he didn’t have any identification,” Torres recalled.
“I couldn’t find anything. The last thing I did was look in the trunk, and there was an invoice from the Nissan dealership with a phone number on it,” he explained.
As luck would have it, the number belonged to Grow’s daughter, Maggie Henkin. Torres called her, helping reunite the 78-year-old with his family.

While waiting for Henkin to arrive, Grow sat down and played music on a piano that Torres had in his front yard.
“Angelo happens to have a piano in his front yard. My dad is a musician. He’s had Alzheimer’s for six years now,” Henkin told NBC.
“But it’s something he does all day. He still remembers how to.”
Neighbors had placed the piano outside Torres’ home after deciding they no longer wanted the instrument.
Grow’s family said they were relieved he was safe and back home in Maryland, where he has resumed playing the piano.
“I’m just so grateful and thankful. It was truly a miracle, and I’m so grateful for Angelo. There are still good people out there,” Henkin said.
Torres said he felt the unlikely chain of events was connected to the memory of his late father.
“All week I was thinking about my dad — you know, my dad was good to me — and then all of a sudden he shows up, and I’m thinking my dad came in this form,” Torres said.
“That’s what I’m thinking.”

sources.news_title: ‘Truly a miracle': Bowie grandfather with Alzheimer's found playing piano hours from home
sources.text:
A Prince George’s County, Maryland, grandfather with Alzheimer’s disease went missing, setting off a frantic police search and a Silver Alert. He turned up outside Philadelphia, playing a piano on a front lawn near his childhood home.
If music is the universal language, you could say Frank Grow loves making a statement. The longtime musician has had Alzheimer’s for six years now, but he still remembers how to play his favorite songs. And last Thursday, he also remembered how much he loves a road trip.
Stream NBC4 newscasts for free right here, right now.
Grow hadn’t driven since his diagnosis, but when his daughter, Maggie Henkin, left the car running outside while she grabbed coffee, he seized his chance.
“I was gone for literally two minutes, and when I came back out, the car was gone,” Henkin said. “I just panicked. I didn’t know how far he had gotten.”
“I was headed away from where I was,” Grow said.
Turns out, he was headed to his childhood home. He made it all the way to Philadelphia but found himself drawn to a different neighborhood, where one of the houses just happened to have a piano on the front lawn.
Angelo Torres found him.

“I pulled up to him and I said, ‘Sir, are you OK? And he said, ‘No, I’m not OK,” Torres said.
Torres dug through Grow’s car to try to find some sort of identification. He managed to find an old receipt with Henkin’s number.
“When Angelo called, I heard my dad in the background saying, ‘Oh, I really did it this time,’” she said.
Torres said his dad passed away six years ago, around the same time Grow was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. Torres said he feels like Grow turning up on his street was a sign from his dad from above.
“It’s incredible how he just got here. Out of thousands of streets he could’ve turned on, it was this street,” Torres said. “So, I think it was meant for me to find him and help him out.”
“Truly a miracle, and I’m just so grateful for Angelo and that there are still good people out there,” Henkin said.
Grow said he doesn’t remember all the details of his trip to Philly. His family will never forget the kindness that kept him safe.
Grow is still in tune with the music and the memories that matter most.
“I love you, Dad,” Henkin said.
“Well, thank you,” he said. “I love you too.”

sources.news_title: Lost In Memory: Elderly Pianist With Alzheimer’s Travels Two States To Find Childhood Home, Discovers Piano In Philadelphia Yard
Missing Grandpa With Alzheimer's Found Playing Piano on a Stranger's Lawn 100 Miles from Home
sources.text:
A Maryland grandfather with Alzheimer’s slipped away in his daughter’s car last week and turned up more than 100 miles from home, sitting at a piano on a stranger’s front lawn. It’s a touching story about Alzheimer’s and music, and about a man in Philadelphia who stopped to ask if he was okay.
Two Minutes Is All It Takes
Frank Grow is 78 and lives in Bowie, Maryland. He’s a longtime musician and has lived with Alzheimer’s for six years now. But he still remembers how to play his favorite songs.
His daughter Maggie Henkin cares for him. Frank hadn’t driven since his diagnosis. Then on Thursday, Nov. 19, Maggie left the car running outside while she grabbed coffee.
“I was gone for literally two minutes, and when I came back out, the car was gone,” she told NBC4 Washington. “I just panicked. I didn’t know how far he had gotten.”
His disappearance set off a Silver Alert and a frantic police search, and Bowie police put out a critical missing person report. Sitting beside his daughter later, Frank told the reporter, “I’ve stopped driving.” He was gently reminded, “You did, but then you took the car.” His reply was honest. “That’s true.” And when it came to where he was going, Frank kept it simple: “I was headed away from where I was.”
Frank Drives All the Way to Philadelphia
Frank was trying to find his childhood home in Norristown, Pennsylvania, just outside Philadelphia. He drove across the Bay Bridge and made it all the way into the city. But he ended up on a residential street in Northeast Philadelphia instead.
On that street an old piano was sitting in the front yard of Angelo Torres’ home. Neighbors had put it out there to give it away. Frank found it, sat down and started to play.
“Sir, Are You Okay?”
Angelo noticed Frank standing on the corner and could tell something was wrong. “I pulled up to him and I said, ‘Sir, are you okay?’ And he said, ‘No, I’m not okay,'” Angelo told NBC4.
Most of us would have kept driving past an older man on a street corner. Angelo pulled over and asked a simple question.
In the video Angelo recorded, Frank smiles as he plays the piano on the grass. “That’s my friend Frank,” Angelo says. “I just met him.”
Frank had no ID on him. So Angelo checked the Nissan Sentra and found an old invoice in the trunk with Maggie’s phone number on it. Around 1 p.m. Maggie got a call from an unknown Philadelphia number.
“When Angelo called, I heard my dad in the background saying, ‘Oh, I really did it this time,'” she said. Then she told Angelo, “Yes, that’s my dad.”
“It Was This Street”
Angelo still can’t get over where Frank ended up. “It’s incredible how he just got here. Out of thousands of streets he could’ve turned on, it was this street,” he said. “So, I think it was meant for me to find him and help him out.”
There’s one more detail that makes this even more special. Angelo’s own father passed away about six years ago, around the same time Frank was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. Angelo said he had been thinking about his dad all week, and Frank showing up on his street felt like a sign.
“Truly a miracle, and I’m just so grateful for Angelo and that there are still good people out there,” Maggie said.
Frank Is Home and Playing Piano Again
Frank is back home with his family and playing the piano again. He doesn’t remember all the details of his trip to Philly, but his family won’t forget the kindness that kept him safe. For any family watching Alzheimer’s slowly take memories away, it’s a gentle reminder of how much music can still mean to the people we love.
At the end of the report Maggie told her dad, “I love you, Dad.” Frank answered, “Well, thank you. I love you too.”
That short moment between them says so much. Frank may forget roads and dates, but he still knows his daughter’s love, and he gives it right back. Maggie cares for her dad, and you can hear in her voice how much he means to her. You don’t see that kind of bond between a parent and child very often these days. So many of us get caught up in our own lives, and time with our aging parents slowly slips down the list. Maggie and Frank are a beautiful picture of what family can look like.
Music Stays When Other Memories Fade
Frank can’t always remember where he is going, but he still remembers his favorite songs. Doctors say that is common. According to Mayo Clinic, musical memories are often preserved in Alzheimer’s because the parts of the brain linked to musical memory are relatively undamaged by the disease. A 2015 study published in the medical journal Brain found that musical memory is surprisingly strong in people with Alzheimer’s, even in advanced stages.
Music helps in other ways too. Mayo Clinic says listening to or singing songs can relieve stress, ease anxiety and depression, and reduce agitation in people with dementia. It also gives families a way to connect with a loved one who finds it hard to talk. Maybe that is why Frank looked so happy sitting at that piano after such a long and confusing drive.
God Directs Our Steps
Frank planned to go to his childhood home in Norristown. He could have kept driving for hours, getting more and more lost. But on that street, a piano was sitting in a front yard, and it stopped him right there. A man who has loved music all his life found the one thing that would make him sit down and stay. I believe God placed that piano there. The neighbors only put it out to give it away, but God knew Frank would come down that street. And He made sure a man willing to stop was there too. That is not luck. That is God at work.
Proverbs 16:9 says, “A man’s heart plans his way, But the LORD directs his steps.” Maggie didn’t know where her dad was for those hours, but God knew exactly where he was the whole time. And He used an ordinary man who simply pulled over and asked a question.
There are people around us right now who are confused, lost or just not okay, and most of them won’t say it first. Let’s be the ones who slow down and ask, “Are you okay?” God may have put them on our street for a reason.

sources.news_title: Maryland Man With Alzheimer's Found in Northeast Philadelphia
sources.text:
A 78-year-old Maryland man living with Alzheimer’s disease ended up standing alone on a Northeast Philadelphia street corner last week, more than 100 miles from his home in Bowie, with no identification and no way to explain how he got there. He was found safe. The reason he made the trip at all traces back to a childhood home in Norristown that he was trying to reach.
A Search That Started With a Simple Question
Frank Grow had lived with Alzheimer’s disease for six years before he left his Bowie home on a Thursday, according to NBC10 Philadelphia. He was reportedly seeking out the Norristown house where he grew up, but instead traveled more than 100 miles and ended up on a residential street in Northeast Philadelphia. It was there that Angelo Torres spotted him standing on a corner and pulled over to check on him.
Grow’s attempt to reach a childhood home fits a broader pattern: wandering can involve someone with dementia becoming lost while trying to get somewhere familiar. The Alzheimer’s Association estimates six in 10 people living with dementia wander at least once, and says it can happen at any stage of the disease. The organization warns that getting lost can be dangerous or life-threatening.
Torres recalled the moment plainly: “I noticed a gentleman standing on the corner. So I pulled up to him and asked, ‘Sir, are you OK?’ and he said, ‘No, I’m not OK,’” per the outlet’s report. Grow had no identification on him, leaving Torres with little to go on as he tried to figure out who the man was and how to get him home.
A Car Trunk Clue Cracks the Case
Torres searched for any way to identify Grow and reach his family. He found it in an unlikely place: an invoice from a Nissan dealership tucked in the trunk of Grow’s car, which carried a phone number. Using that number, Torres was able to contact Grow’s daughter, Maggie Henkin, who was more than 100 miles away in Bowie at the time, the same outlet reported.
When she heard the description, Henkin didn’t hesitate. “Yes, that’s my dad,” she said, confirming the man Torres had found was indeed her father. The reunion that followed brought relief after an ordeal that left the family not knowing where he was.
Maryland has a Silver Alert program for missing adults with cognitive impairments, including Alzheimer’s disease or dementia, when their disappearance poses a credible threat to their health and safety. State criteria also require the person to be entered into the National Crime Information Center; only law enforcement can request an alert. Maryland State Police says there is no waiting period to report a missing person.
A Piano, a Memory, and a Family's Gratitude
Grow is described as a musician who still remembers how to play the piano despite his Alzheimer’s diagnosis, and he continues to play at home, the report notes. In the neighborhood where he was found, neighbors had placed a piano out in a front yard for anyone to take, a detail tying together the unexpected stop on his journey. Grow returned safely home with his family afterward.
Henkin expressed her gratitude for the stranger who stepped in without hesitation. “I’m just so grateful and thankful. It was truly a miracle and I’m so grateful for Angelo and there are still good people out there,” she said. Her words captured both the fear of the hours her father was missing and the relief of a safe ending made possible by one person’s willingness to stop and ask if a stranger needed help.
